title: Annual Fraud Report 2026 (covering 2025 data)
notes: Defines eight APP scam types (malicious payee: purchase, investment, romance, advance fee; malicious redirection: invoice and mandate, CEO, impersonation police/bank staff, impersonation other) with 2025 values: total APP £576.4m (+19%) across 248,070 cases; total fraud £1.28bn. Describes safe-account and 'undercover operation' police/bank impersonation, purchase scams moved off-platform to bank transfer, romance averaging 9.7 payments per scam, and courier scams where cards are handed over on the doorstep.

title: APP fraud reimbursement protections (consumer information)
date: undated (protections apply to payments on or after 7 October 2024)
notes: Since 7 Oct 2024, individuals, microenterprises and charities who lose money over Faster Payments or CHAPS to an APP scam should be reimbursed up to £85,000 (optional excess up to £100, not for vulnerable consumers), claimed within 13 months, normally within 5 business days (max 35 with stop-the-clock). Exceptions are complicity, gross negligence (not applied to vulnerable consumers) and civil disputes; customers are expected to heed bank warnings and respond to bank information requests.

title: One year on: impact of APP reimbursement on victims
notes: Reports that in the first nine months (Oct 2024-Jun 2025) £112 million was returned and 88% of money lost to APP scams and claimed back was reimbursed (up from 66% a year earlier); 126,000 claims were made, 84% resolved within five business days.

title: A-Z of cyber crime and fraud
publisher: Report Fraud (City of London Police; formerly Action Fraud)
notes: Old actionfraud.police.uk/a-z-of-fraud URL now redirects here (WebFetch blocked with 403; read via browser). Lists UK police fraud types including 419 emails, auction/shopping fraud, courier fraud, cryptocurrency investment fraud, holiday, inheritance, lottery, loan scams, mandate/payment diversion fraud (BEC), recovery fraud, rental, recruitment, romance fraud (also called 'pig butchering'), sextortion, smishing, ticket fraud, vishing and work-from-home scams.

title: Report Fraud: new service from City of London Police
publisher: GOV.UK (Home Office / City of London Police)
notes: Report Fraud replaced Action Fraud as the national fraud and cyber crime reporting platform from 4 December 2025; phone 0300 123 2040 unchanged, website reportfraud.police.uk, old Action Fraud web traffic redirected.

title: Consumer Sentinel Network Data Book 2024
notes: Latest full Data Book listed on ftc.gov (no 2025 edition found at the expected URL, which returned 404). Reports 2.6 million fraud reports and over $12 billion lost in 2024; 845,806 imposter scam reports with $2.95 billion lost; bank transfers/payments had the highest aggregate losses ($2.09 billion) followed by cryptocurrency ($1.42 billion), while credit cards were most often reported; median loss for investment-related fraud $9,196.

title: Prepared Statement of the FTC on The Rising Scam Economy, Joint Economic Committee
notes: Gives full-year 2025 Sentinel figures: 3 million fraud reports and $15.9 billion reported lost; over 1 million imposter reports with over $3.5 billion lost; investment scams over $7.9 billion (about half of all losses). Bank payments had the highest aggregate losses, followed by cryptocurrency; text messages were the top reported contact method and social media the top contact method by losses (over $2 billion in FY 2025).

title: FTC Data Show People Reported Losing $3.5 Billion to Imposter Scams in 2025
notes: Reports $3.5 billion lost to imposter scams in 2025, nearly one in three fraud reports; government impersonators about $920 million (up from $789 million in 2024) and business impersonators nearly $1 billion (up from $866 million), with bank impersonators the highest-loss business imposters; total 2025 fraud losses about $16 billion.

title: Types of scams
notes: WebFetch returned 403; read in a browser. Lists contact channels (text/SMS, phone, email, social media, website, in-person) and 13 scam types: gambling and betting, phishing, relationship, investment, account or identity takeover, buying and selling, threat, jobs and employment, unexpected money, business email compromise, money recovery, donation scams. Notes text scams can impersonate government, businesses or family and friends.

title: Continued action critical to combat fraud as annual scam losses exceed $2 billion (Targeting Scams Report 2025)
notes: For calendar 2025, 481,523 combined scam reports, 274,577 with losses totalling $2.18 billion (losses up 7.8% on 2024, down 29.7% from the 2022 peak). Top five by loss: investment ($837.7m), payment re-direction ($166.8m), romance ($139.9m), phishing ($97.6m), remote access ($69.9m). People 65+ were 26.5% of Scamwatch losses; text-message scam reports fell from 77,365 to 29,058. The full report PDF (nasc.gov.au) blocked fetching.

title: Mid-Year Scam and Cybercrime Brief 2026
notes: 1H 2026: 16,821 scam cases (-14.4%), about S$410.6 million lost (-17.9%); 80.8% of scams involved self-effected transfers. Top 10 table gives cases/losses for e-commerce, phishing, investment, job, government officials impersonation (GOIS: 1,363 cases, S$90.8M), social media impersonation, sexual services, loan, internet love and fake friend call scams (353 cases, S$818K). Describes GOIS as bank/telco caller hand-off to fake MAS/MinLaw/SPF officers demanding transfers to 'safety accounts' or cash/gold handovers, plus BEC gift-card variant and courier-redelivery phishing.

title: Understanding scam types
publisher: ScamShield (Singapore National Crime Prevention Council / SPF)
notes: Read in a browser (old /scams/ URL 404s for WebFetch). Lists 12 scam types: government officials impersonation, investment, job, e-commerce, phishing, fake friend call, loan, tech support, insurance service, internet love, sexual service and cryptocurrency-related scams; states crypto-related scams caused S$182.2M losses in 2025 (20% of reported losses). Tech support entry warns never to grant remote access or approve bank transactions for unsolicited callers.

title: Scams and Cybercrime Fell by Almost a Quarter in 2025
notes: Summarises the Annual Scams and Cybercrime Brief 2025: scam and cybercrime cases down 24.8% to 41,974; losses S$913.1 million (from S$1.1 billion in 2024); top five by losses were investment, government official impersonation, job, phishing and BEC scams; 81.8% of scams involved self-effected transfers; fake friend call cases and losses fell significantly.

title: The seven words that reveal you're talking to a scammer: 'Move your money to a safe account'
notes: Lloyds data (Jul 2025-Jun 2026): impersonation scam victims lost £3,516 on average (+10%); HMRC (+63%), broadband/mobile (+57%), solicitor (+35%), Amazon (+27%) and police/bank (+4%) impersonation rose while all impersonation fell 3%; bank and police impersonation up 18% in Q2 2026. Says criminals tell victims their own bank is involved in fraud and coach them to lie to genuine bank staff; case study of an 85-year-old told by fake police not to contact her bank, who bought £188,000 of gold collected by a fake undercover officer. Read via browser (WebFetch hit an error page).

title: Keep yourself safe from safe account scams
notes: Safe account scammers impersonate banks, police, the National Crime Agency or an internet provider, may start with smishing/phishing, and may claim the real bank is under investigation and tell victims to lie if their bank calls; some ask for remote access software or cite an overpayment or loan. States no bank, law enforcement or internet provider will ask you to move money to keep it safe; call 159.

title: Santander's Head Of Fraud targeted as impersonation scams rise by 11%
notes: Describes spoofed calls/texts using a real employee's name (victims told to look the person up on LinkedIn), a claim the account is compromised, and instructions to move money to a 'safe account' and to lie about the payment purpose so the bank cannot give a relevant warning. Santander impersonation losses £10.2 million in Jan-Mar 2023 (+11%), average loss £6,906.

title: Ombudsman's final decision DRN8143231 (Miss R v Lloyds Bank PLC, HMRC impersonation)
notes: A fake HMRC caller (spoofing HMRC's real number) threatened a 63-year-old with arrest over unpaid tax, told her not to reveal the real reason because the bank would close her account, and told her to say the money was for a holiday on a prepaid travel card; she repeated this cover story to Lloyds' fraud team and branch while the scammer listened via her phone in her handbag. The ombudsman notes it is widely recognised fraudsters instruct customers to give a cover story and that banks should probe further.

title: Courier fraud (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
publisher: Report Fraud (City of London Police; formerly Action Fraud)
notes: Fake police/bank callers claim a fraudulent card payment, expiring card, corrupt bank staff or a crooked jeweller/currency exchange, then ask victims to withdraw cash, buy expensive items or hand over card and PIN to a courier; they keep the landline open when victims 'call back'. Victims may be told not to discuss it with anyone and to lie to their bank or bypass its security measures. Read via browser (WebFetch 403).

title: Over 70s targeted as courier fraud exceeds £21 million in 2025, with London and Home Counties hit hardest
publisher: Report Fraud / City of London Police
notes: Courier fraud reports rose from 1,721 (2024) to 1,891 (2025); losses from £19.5 million to more than £21 million; average £15,311.08 per victim. People aged 76-96 account for about 62% of reports; London and surrounding regions about 65% of victims. Growing 2025 trend of victims buying gold/jewellery at multiple jewellers over time for a courier, with contact kept up via WhatsApp for days or weeks.

title: Phishing and scams: report HMRC related phishing emails, texts and phone call scams
date: First published 14 May 2025; last updated 24 November 2025
notes: HMRC will never send a tax rebate notification or ask for personal or payment details by text, never offers rebates via social media, and only emails from addresses ending hmrc.gov.uk. Report texts to 60599, emails to phishing@hmrc.gov.uk and calls via the online suspicious-call form.

title: Tax scams / consumer alerts
notes: Warning signs of IRS impersonators: demands for immediate payment with 'now or else' pressure, threats of arrest or deportation, no chance to question or appeal the amount, and unexpected fake tax bills.

title: How To Avoid a Government Impersonation Scam
notes: Scammers pose as SSA (number 'suspended', benefits ending), IRS (taxes owed, arrest/deportation/licence threats), Medicare, the FTC or police/courts (warrants, missed jury duty), and may tell you to move money to keep it safe or withdraw cash/buy gold to hand over. The government will never demand payment by wire, gift card, cryptocurrency or payment app, threaten arrest, or suspend your SSN; the IRS does not call about taxes without prior mailed notices.

title: Impersonation scams: not what they used to be (Data Spotlight)
notes: 2023: over 330,000 business-impersonation and nearly 160,000 government-impersonation reports, combined losses over $1.1 billion (more than 3x 2020). Describes multi-hop scams (fake Amazon to fake bank to fake FBI/FTC), fake security alerts, Geek Squad renewals with fake refund 'overpayments', bogus legal problems, and victims told to move money or load cash into Bitcoin ATMs ('safety lockers') to protect it.

title: Scam alerts
notes: Read in a browser (WebFetch 403). ATO impersonation via email, SMS, calls, social media and fake sites, including 2026 variants: malware 'payment update' emails installing remote desktop software, fake appointment emails with myGov phishing, and a crypto 'non-KYC wallet' email demanding an immediate declaration call. The ATO will never threaten arrest or prosecution via email/SMS or request payment or personal details through unsolicited communication; verify on 1800 008 540.

title: ACCC warning of suspicious messages as "Hi Mum" scams spike
notes: More than 1,150 Australians lost $2.6 million to 'Hi Mum' scams in the first seven months of 2022, mostly via WhatsApp: the scammer claims a lost or broken phone and new number, builds rapport, then asks for money for an urgent bill, contractor or new phone because they cannot access online banking. 82% of reports came from people over 55, accounting for 95% of losses; advice is to call the number already stored in your phone.

title: Scammers Use Fake Emergencies To Steal Your Money
notes: Family emergency scammers pose as a relative in trouble (sometimes with an AI-cloned voice) or as a lawyer, police officer or doctor, stress urgency, and ask you to keep it secret; they ask for wire transfers, crypto, payment apps or gift card numbers. Advice: hang up, call the relative on a known number and check with others even if told to keep it secret.

title: 2025 IC3 Annual Report
date: 2026 (covers calendar 2025; release date not printed in extracted text)
notes: 2025: 1,008,597 complaints, $20.877 billion losses (+26%); 60+ filed 201,266 complaints with $7.7 billion losses. Top cyber-enabled fraud by loss: investment $8.65bn, BEC $3.05bn, tech support $2.13bn, confidence/romance $929m, government impersonation $798m; crypto investment fraud $7.2bn. Crypto ATM/kiosk: 13,460 complaints, $389 million (+58%), 60+ lost $257.5m; recovery scams 10,516 complaints, $1.4 billion; gold courier scams about 725 complaints, $311.8 million.

title: Business email compromise scams
notes: Scammers pretend to be a business you use and send an invoice with new payee details so a legitimate payment is redirected; warning signs are unexpected bills, supplier payment details changing without notice and slightly altered email addresses. Advice: call the business on an independently sourced number before paying changed details. Read via browser.

title: How To Spot, Avoid, and Report Tech Support Scams
notes: Fake pop-ups, calls, texts and search ads lead victims to fake technicians who seek remote access. A refund variant uses fake Geek Squad/McAfee/Norton renewal notices; the caller 'processes a refund', claims too much was refunded and asks the victim to send back the difference by gift card, wire/bank transfer, crypto or payment app. Real security warnings never ask you to call a number.

title: Tech Support Scams
notes: Pop-ups with local-looking numbers lead to fake Microsoft/Apple support who get victims to install AnyDesk, UltraViewer or ConnectWise, log into banking and approve transactions with digital tokens so money can be moved out. Microsoft and Apple never send pop-ups asking you to call; never install remote access apps for unsolicited callers.

title: False alarm, real scam: how scammers are stealing older adults' life savings (Data Spotlight)
notes: Reports from older adults losing $10,000+ to business/government impersonators rose from 1,790 (2020) to 8,269 (2024); $100K+ reports rose nearly sevenfold. Storylines: account misuse, information tied to a crime, or computer security problem (fake pop-ups), with hand-offs between fake bank/Amazon/Microsoft/SSA/FTC agents; victims are told to transfer money, deposit cash into Bitcoin ATMs or hand cash/gold to couriers, and kept on the phone. Payment methods for $10K+ losses: crypto 33%, bank transfer 20%, cash 16%.

title: Romance fraud (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
notes: Romance fraud (also called 'pig butchering') uses fake personas; fraudsters require urgency or secrecy and isolate victims from family and friends, and for almost a third of victims the fraud spans more than a year. Advises never sending money (including vouchers, crypto or 'investments') to an online-only partner and being wary of anyone who asks you not to tell others about them; warns of follow-up recovery fraud. Read via browser.

title: Romance scammers' favorite lies exposed (Data Spotlight)
notes: 2022: nearly 70,000 romance scam reports, $1.3 billion lost, median $4,400; crypto and bank wires over 60% of losses, gift cards most frequent method (24%). Common lies: stationed at a faraway military base, offshore oil rig worker, sick/hurt/in jail, crypto investment tutor, package stuck in customs; 40% of losers were first contacted on social media, conversations moved to WhatsApp, Google Chat or Telegram.

title: Internet Love Scams
notes: Scammers build weeks or months of online relationship via fake profiles, avoid video calls and meetings, then cite emergencies (business/financial trouble, immigration, rent, oil rigs, machinery, workers' salaries) or fake investments and repeatedly ask for money. Advice: never transfer money or send gift cards to someone you have not met in person.

title: Ombudsman's final decision DRN-4831389 (Mrs R v HSBC UK Bank Plc, safe account scam)
notes: A fake HSBC fraud-team caller (June 2023) had the victim move £9,150 to another person's account 'to keep it safe', using the reference 'god son' and the payment type 'paying friends or family'; when HSBC's genuine fraud team called, she said it was for her godson's university fees as the scammer had told her. HSBC told the ombudsman customers are sometimes coached on what story to give the bank.

title: Ombudsman's final decision DRN-5540935 (Mrs W v Barclays Bank UK PLC, investment scam cash withdrawal)
notes: An investment scam victim (fake 'Adams Street Partners') withdrew £7,100 cash in branch in April 2024 and gave it to a 'courier'; she told Barclays it was for 'home renovation'. The ombudsman found the scammer had given her a cover story and told her to lie about the payment purpose, and that she confirmed to a Barclays agent no one had told her to mislead the bank.

title: Cryptocurrency investment fraud (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
notes: Calls crypto investment fraud one of the fastest-growing UK fraud types: social media ads often featuring celebrities, or search ads, lead to professional-looking sites that manipulate prices and returns; victims usually discover the fraud when trying to sell. Red flags are unexpected contact, pressure to invest quickly and unrealistic returns; check firms on the FCA Financial Services Register. Read via browser.

title: Holiday fraud (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
notes: Fake adverts, sales calls and messages offer very cheap holidays or short-term lets using stolen property photos, and tell people to pay in cash or by bank transfer or money transfer services that are hard to trace; victims discover at the airport or hotel that nothing was booked. Red flag: being asked to pay by bank transfer or cash; advice is to pay by credit card and check ABTA/ATOL membership. Read via browser.

title: Inheritance fraud (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
notes: A fake overseas lawyer says someone with your surname died leaving a fortune and offers to split it; the fraudsters stress secrecy and speed, then demand successive taxes, legal and banking fees, inventing reasons each time why fees cannot come out of the inheritance and pressuring reluctant victims with how much they have already paid. Read via browser.

title: Unexpected money scams
notes: Covers inheritance, rebate, scratchie, travel prize, money transfer and lottery/prize scams in which victims are told they are owed money and must pay an upfront fee, tax or 'administration fee' or share financial/identity details. Government departments and trusted companies never ask for upfront payment to claim a grant or rebate. Read via browser.

title: Got a text about unpaid tolls? It's probably a scam
notes: Texts posing as tolling agencies claim unpaid tolls with an amount and a link to a page harvesting card/bank details and personal data such as driver's licence numbers. Advice: do not click, check with the tolling agency via a known number or site, report junk or forward to 7726.

title: Smishing (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
notes: Fake texts (SMS, WhatsApp) lure victims to sites that steal data and money; senders can spoof numbers so messages sit in a genuine bank's thread. Red flags include a delivery company demanding a fee before delivering a parcel, urgent security alerts, and family appeals for money; forward to 7726. Read via browser.

title: Avoiding and Reporting Gift Card Scams
notes: Scammers posing as government agencies, Microsoft/Apple support, family members (sometimes voice-cloned), prize organisers, utilities, romantic interests or fake-check senders demand gift cards (Google Play, Apple, Amazon, eBay, Target); they tell victims to buy at several stores so cashiers won't get suspicious, stay on the phone, and send the number and PIN or a photo. No real business or agency will tell you to pay with a gift card.

title: Money recovery scams
notes: Scammers contact previous victims posing as government agencies, lawyers, police or charities, or run recovery websites and ads, offering to recover stolen money (including tracing crypto) for a fee, percentage or 'tax', then ask for more money for the 'investigation', personal details and remote access. Advice: never accept offers to get your money back; work with your bank. Read via browser.

title: Refund and Recovery Scams
notes: Recovery scammers buy 'sucker lists' of past victims and pose as government agencies, consumer groups or law firms, demanding upfront retainer, processing, tax or shipping fees or bank/card numbers to 'deposit' a refund. The FTC and real agencies never charge fees to help you get a refund, never ask for financial details for this, and never guarantee recovery.

title: Fake Friend Call Scams
notes: Scammers call or WhatsApp from an unknown number, ask the victim to 'guess who' they are, claim a lost phone and new number, then ask for urgent 'loans' for renovation contractors, new-business costs or suppliers, paid via PayNow to unknown persons' accounts; some ask victims to click links or install apps. Advice: verify by calling the friend's last known number. Read via browser.

title: Government Officials Impersonation Scams
notes: Unsolicited calls or WhatsApp video calls from fake SPF or MAS officers accuse victims of crimes and instruct them to transfer money to a 'safe account' for 'investigations', or hand over cash, gold or luxury watches at meet-ups, or show IDs and bank cards on video. Government officials will never ask you to transfer money, disclose bank log-ins, install unofficial apps or transfer your call to the Police; overseas police have no powers to require Singapore residents to assist without government approval. Read via browser.

title: Paying to get paid: gamified job scams drive record losses (Data Spotlight)
notes: Job scam losses topped $220 million in 1H 2024; about 20,000 task-scam reports in 1H 2024 vs about 5,000 in all of 2023; crypto losses to job scams about $41 million in 1H 2024. Task scams start with unexpected texts/WhatsApp messages, pay small early commissions for liking videos or rating products in sets of forty, then require deposits (mostly crypto) to unlock tasks or withdraw; fake group chats pressure hesitant victims.

title: Jobs and employment scams
notes: Fake recruiters (posing as big brands, online shopping platforms or agencies) contact people via text, WhatsApp, Signal or Telegram offering easy work-from-home income with no interview, then require them to top up an account with their own money or crypto (USDT) to complete tasks, pay recruitment/training fees, or move money and packages for others (money mules). Advice: never pay to get a job. Read via browser.

title: Bitcoin ATMs: A payment portal for scammers (Data Spotlight)
notes: Reported Bitcoin ATM fraud losses rose nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023 and topped $65 million in 1H 2024, median loss $10,000; people 60+ were over three times as likely to report a loss and accounted for about 71% ($46 million) of losses. Most cases are government/business impersonation or tech support scams; victims are told to withdraw cash from their bank, go to a specific machine and scan a texted QR code, with the machines called 'safety lockers'.

title: Sextortion (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
notes: Financially motivated sexual extortion: an unknown or hacked account quickly moves to explicit chat on an encrypted app, obtains (or fakes with AI) intimate images, then blackmails the victim for money or gift cards. Advises stopping contact, not paying more (payment invites further demands), keeping evidence and reporting to police (101/999) and the platform. Read via browser.

title: Loan scams (A-Z of cyber crime and fraud)
notes: Loan scams are advance fee fraud: a fast-loan advert approves anyone regardless of credit history, then demands an upfront fee (e.g. 'insurance' for the loan) and disappears. Advice: check the FCA register and avoid bank transfer payments. Read via browser.

title: Loan Scams
notes: Fast cash loan ads on TikTok/Facebook or unsolicited SMS/WhatsApp offers lead victims to pay upfront by iBanking transfer, ATM cash deposit, PayNow or cash handover, and the loan is never disbursed. Licensed moneylenders may not advertise this way and must approve loans in person; never pay upfront fees for a loan. Read via browser.
